paras: The attempted lynching at Evergreen, Alabama, was a siege of the Conecuh County jail by about 100 armed men early on Sunday, August 7, 1910, aimed at Black prisoners held in the killing of an aged farmer, Jesse Baldwin. Company K of the Alabama National Guard refused the mob's demands for the jail keys, and the crowd dispersed without anyone being hurt. The two men charged with the murder, Albert Johnson and John Manuel, were moved to Mobile that afternoon, and wire stories carried the episode nationally as a lynching prevented by troops.

Baldwin, who lived alone in an isolated neighborhood, was found near his home at Wilcox Station about July 7 with his skull crushed by a hoe, and money he was known to keep there was missing. By Saturday, August 6, officers held five Black suspects: Johnson, Charley Henderson, John Manuel, Charley Manuel and Jerry Mims. Johnson reportedly blamed the fatal blow on a man named White, Thomas in one dispatch and Remus in later ones, who had been shot dead by a deputy sheriff during his arrest. On Johnson's capture the Evergreen correspondent wrote that "no violence is anticipated," and Sheriff Irwin later said he thought feeling had cooled when he left for Montgomery on Saturday.

At 10:45 Saturday night a train brought word from Owassa that armed men would attack the jail "with a view to lynching all the negroes concerned in the murder." Captain T. M. Bruner called Company K to its armory, where, according to the militiamen, several mob members demanded the keys from the deputies and were ordered out. The soldiers had barely formed a line around the jail when the mob arrived, about 100 men with shotguns and Winchester rifles, or 100 to 125 in the first report.

Halted forty feet from the line, the crowd sent forward an unnamed leader, who again asked for the keys and was refused. Militiamen said the men cocked their guns and muttered, but after about half an hour they left quietly toward the north. Other reports said the mob fired shots during a siege lasting from 12:30 until after 3 a.m.; no one was reported injured.

Fearing a larger mob, Sheriff Irwin obtained Circuit Judge J. C. Richardson's permission to move Johnson and Manuel, who left under military escort for the Mobile county jail on Sunday afternoon. Militiamen also arrested Frank Mitchell on a train that morning for helping the two evade arrest, the charge the Advertiser said the three remaining prisoners also faced. In Mobile, Johnson told a reporter he had watched the killing but struck no blow, accusing Manuel and White, and Manuel called him a liar. The militia said it recognized none of the mob, "although they were not masked," and no arrest of any mob member appears in the coverage.

The Montgomery Advertiser covered the siege through its own Evergreen correspondent, headlining "SOLDIERS OF CONECUH GUARD BLACK QUINTET" and calling the mob "Angered Citizens." Its second report drew on the militiamen and noted that in Baldwin's neighborhood "feeling is said to be bitter against the negroes." Earlier white headlines had treated the accusation as settled, as in the Birmingham Age-Herald's "Negro Murderer Captured."

On August 8 a wire dispatch ran from Washington to El Paso under headlines such as "MILITIA CALLED OUT TO PREVENT LYNCHINGS" and "LYNCHERS FORESTALLED." It credited Sheriff Irwin with calling out the troops, although the Advertiser placed him in a Montgomery hotel that night. A second wire story, expecting friends of the dead man to "allow the law to take its course," ran in Atlanta as "ARRIVAL OF TROOPS SAVES NEGROES FOM MOB."

The only Black-press coverage found was in the Richmond Planet of August 13, which reprinted that story as "NEGROES SAVED BY THE SOLDIERS" beside the Mobile confession item, "NEGRO CONFESSED TO THE MURDER," without comment.

Reports differ on when the mob gathered, 12:30 a.m. in the Advertiser and the Planet's text but 2:30 a.m. in the first wire version, and the Advertiser's fuller second report does not mention shots. The wire named only Johnson and Manuel as targets, while the Advertiser spoke of five prisoners.

reader.title: Attempted lynching at Evergreen, Alabama (1910)
bases: An armed mob surrounded the Conecuh County jail threatening to lynch Black prisoners accused of murder and was turned back by militia, an attempted lynching (A3, A5, A7).

A mob of about 100 armed men tried to get the jail keys to lynch prisoners accused of killing Jesse Baldwin, but troops held it off and no one was killed (A3, A5, A7); this was an attempted lynching, not a completed one.
The Montgomery Advertiser's own Evergreen specials and two separate wire stories agree that an armed mob surrounded the jail and dispersed when troops appeared (A3, A5, A7, A23).

accounts.label: Montgomery Advertiser Evergreen specials (militiamen's statements)
accounts.gist: About 100 armed men from the Owassa area demanded the jail keys twice, cocked their guns before a line of troops, and left after half an hour; the first report adds occasional shots between 12:30 and after 3 a.m.

accounts.label: First wire report
accounts.gist: A mob gathered at 2:30 a.m. threatening to lynch Johnson and Manuel; Sheriff Irwin forestalled violence by calling the militia and the men went home.

accounts.label: Second wire report
accounts.gist: The mob formed at 12:30 Sunday morning, fired shots and made threats, and dispersed at 3 when troops surrounded the jail; Johnson and Manuel were taken to Mobile.

accounts.label: Albert Johnson's statement in Mobile
accounts.gist: Johnson said he was at Baldwin's house and saw the killing but struck no blow, naming Manuel and White; Manuel called him a liar.

framing.detail: The Montgomery Advertiser headlined 'SOLDIERS OF CONECUH GUARD BLACK QUINTET' and called the mob 'Angered Citizens', reported that feeling was 'bitter against the negroes', and credited the militia with averting 'serious consequence'.
Out-of-state papers ran the wire under 'MILITIA CALLED OUT TO PREVENT LYNCHINGS', 'LYNCHERS FORESTALLED', 'ALABAMA MILITIA PREVENTS LYNCHING' and 'Repels a Mob'.
Before the mob, white headlines treated Johnson's guilt as settled: 'Negro Murderer Captured', 'CHASE FOR NEGRO ENDS'.
The Richmond Planet reprinted the wire under 'NEGROES SAVED BY THE SOLDIERS' and the confession item as 'NEGRO CONFESSED TO THE MURDER', with no editorial comment.
